Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky says he faces the same label once given to Steve Jobs at Apple: ‘I think some peo
sum: True to that style, Chesky spends three hours a day recruiting and has told his hiring managers they can leave if they do not like his input. Still, he insists that staying closely involved in the details is not the same as micromanaging.

To better understand how Jobs operated, Chesky once asked former Apple design chief Jony Ive, who worked closely with Jobs for nearly 15 years on iconic products including the iMac, iPod, iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, what it was actually like to work for him.

“Johny said to me, ‘I never felt like Steve was micromanaging,’” Chesky recalled. Instead, Ive felt the two were “constantly partnering” because Jobs had lunch with him every day and wanted to be immersed in the details rather than simply ordering him around.

For Chesky, that distinction defines where he draws the line at Airbnb. Chesky views traditional micromanagement, which is telling employees exactly what to do, as a last resort and a sign that someone is struggling in their role.
“If I’m telling somebody what to do, they’re probably not successful,” he explained, adding that he prefers to partner with teams by asking questions like, “What if we did this? What if we did that?”

Previously, Chesky spoke about how he followed Jobs to bring his company back from the brink of bankruptcy. When the travel industry came to a halt during the 2020 pandemic, Airbnb's planned IPO was derailed and its revenue fell by 72%. The company was just 12 weeks away from insolvency. To pull the business back from the brink, Chesky turned to the blueprint Jobs had used at Apple.
To steer Airbnb out of its tailspin, Chesky said he studied how Steve Jobs salvaged Apple when it was similarly three months from financial ruin.

sum: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky tells everyone that why it is 'impossible' to replace a CEO; says: CEO role may get filled, but what cannot be replaced is role they play as ...

Chesky is of the view that the problem in replacing the founder CEO is not necessarily finding someone to occupy the chief executive's office. But, the main challenge lies in replacing the unique product leadership which founders bring to the table and which highlights in the growth of the company. He also emphasised that founders also posses a deep understanding of the product and its origin, evolution and long-term vision, all these factors nebula them to make decisions which are difficult for any other to replicate. "When they leave, the CEO role gets filled, but the product role they played rarely does," Chesky said.

Chesky's remarks come at a time when founder succession has been in the spotlight following recent developments at Nvidia. The AI chipmaker's founder, Jensen Huang, recently returned to the CEO role after a brief departure, a move that sparked discussions among investors about leadership succession and the challenges of replacing influential founders.

Like many prominent technology founders, Huang has long been closely associated with Nvidia's product roadmap and technological vision. Industry observers frequently credit him with helping steer the company from a graphics-chip maker into the dominant supplier of AI accelerators powering the current artificial intelligence boom.

Chesky's argument suggests that while a board can appoint a new CEO, replacing a founder's deep institutional knowledge and product instincts is far more difficult, particularly at technology companies where innovation and product strategy are closely tied to the personality and vision of the founder.

The post fits a view Chesky has long held. In an interview with Nilay Patel, he said succession planning is hard because great product visionaries tend to be young, and companies lean toward senior functional experts, who usually are not product people. He said Apple should go back to having a CEO who is also the chief product officer, and that the only effective way to get a big company led by a young CEO is for that CEO to be a founder.

sum: “Range matters now”: Microsoft’s Puneet Chandok, GrowthSchool’s Vaibhav Sisinty on the skills that will define Gen Z careers

Airbnb is looking to expand its footprint in India by tapping demand for travel to emerging destinations, increasing the availability of homestays and bringing more local entrepreneurs into the tourism sector, PTI reported.

The company plans to strengthen its accommodation offerings across established leisure markets and metropolitan cities while exploring opportunities in spiritual, cultural and nature-focused destinations, Amanpreet Bajaj, Airbnb's Country Manager for India, told PTI.

The expansion comes as domestic travel accounts for a growing share of bookings by Indian customers. More than 85 per cent of bookings made by Indian guests during the first half of 2026 were for domestic trips. Nearly 70 per cent of first-time bookers during the same period belonged to Gen Z, Bajaj said.

Airbnb is looking to attract travellers to destinations beyond popular holiday markets such as Goa and established hill stations. Locations including Kangra, East Khasi Hills and Srinagar are seeing growing interest, alongside hill stations in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand. Varanasi and Amritsar are also gaining attention as cultural and spiritual travel destinations.
A key part of the strategy involves developing India's homestay sector and helping more people participate in the hospitality business.

Airbnb has a two-year memorandum of understanding with the Ministry of Tourism to support this effort. The initiative includes training hosts, helping them register digitally on the platform and promoting emerging destinations.

From Airbnb’s IPO to a $1 billion stake, the rise of Krishna Rao as CFO of Anthropic
sum: Krishna Rao has been through two tech IPOs in six years. At Airbnb, he worked in finance and business development as the travel company went public during the pandemic. At Anthropic, he is the chief financial officer. The listing of the company behind Claude has also made the Indian-origin executive a billionaire on paper.

Rao holds about 9.5 million Anthropic shares, according to the company’s updated IPO prospectus filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. At $111.50 a share, that holding is worth about $1.06 billion. The prospectus shows he is keeping his entire stake through the offering.

The filing also details an earlier grant of options to buy 14 million Class A shares at $1.30 apiece. At the end of 2025, about 5.7 million of his options were exercisable, with another 8.16 million yet to become exercisable. His reported compensation for the year was $720,250, including a base salary of $706,250.

Rao joined Anthropic in April 2024 after two CFO jobs in very different businesses. The first was at Cedar, a healthcare technology company. The second was at Fanatics Commerce, which sells sports merchandise online.

Before either of those roles, he had spent nearly six years at Airbnb, where his jobs included overseeing financial planning and analysis and leading global corporate and business development. A Yale and Harvard alumnus, he began his career at Bain and spent four years in private equity at Blackstone.

Airbnb’s December 2020 listing came as investors were trying to gauge when people would travel again. Anthropic’s IPO presents a different question. The company spends money on computing power to train its AI models and incurs costs each time customers use them. For shareholders, that makes the cost of serving a growing customer base as important as how much revenue Claude can bring in.

The IPO gives investors a public price for Rao’s stake. It also puts his work as finance chief under greater scrutiny. At Airbnb, Rao’s remit spanned forecasting and finding opportunities for the company to grow. At Anthropic, he will have to explain to public shareholders how fast the company can grow and what it will cost to keep up.

sum: Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky praised Chinese AI models, calling them 'Fast and Cheap'; now US government may ask the company to share his 'China preference' with all Americans
US government proposal aims to 'name and shame' companies using Chinese AI

The proposal is said to show that officials are looking at ways to discourage companies use of Chinese AI models through a "name and shame" campaign while sticking to a broader anti-regulation stance on AI.

The consideration comes as Chinese-made open-weight models are gaining ground with US companies because they are cheaper than proprietary AI tools from top US labs OpenAI and Anthropic, and perform well enough. This has worried China hawks, who fear that Beijing is using such models — like Moonshot AI's Kimi, DeepSeek or Qwen — to hook US companies so they will become dependent on Chinese AI.

In July, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the Trump administration could sanction Chinese AI companies if they were found to be guilty of intellectual property theft via distillation of American models. Distillation is the process of training smaller AI models using the output of larger ones as part of an effort to lower the costs of training a powerful new AI tool.

The issue reportedly attracted the attention of Congress. Republican US Representatives Andrew Garbarino of New York and John Moolenaar of Michigan, who chair the House Homeland Security Committee and the House select committee on China, respectively, launched an investigation into American companies' use of Chinese AI this year.

In an interview to Bloomberg TV in May this year, Chesky clarified that Airbnb is not a customer of Alibaba or other Chinese companies. “We are not providing data to any Chinese companies. They don’t have access to any data,” he said. Airbnb CEO further added, “We’re primarily using a variety of open-source models, including U.S. open-source models. An open-source model does not have access to data. It doesn’t work that way. I think people need to understand how this stuff works.”

sum: It should be a given that if you’re residing somewhere, you should feel secure with your belongings. However, one Airbnb guest was left out of pocket after over $20,000 of possessions were allegedly stolen.
Isla Moon (@isla.moonadventures), who has 1.8 million TikTok followers, explained in a video that she woke up to find that $20,000 of film gear was gone.
“The worst part is that they broke in using the key,” she explained.

Moon then provided more context. She said that her Airbnb was in a big building, and that she and her partner were staying on the 18th floor. But the robber wasn’t a typical burglar. According to Moon, someone who works in the building broke in using the master key. She said she locked all the doors the night before. However, the next morning, the creator said the door was unlocked and her stuff was gone. Apparently, her partner heard someone between midnight and 4am. But because he thought it was Moon, he didn’t see any reason for alarm.
“And guess what,” Moon added. “Airbnb is doing nothing about it.”

Because of this incident, Moon says she left four nights early because she felt unsafe. However, she claims Airbnb won’t refund the stay. Despite submitting a detailed claim, the creator says that Airbnb won’t do anything because, apparently, the host isn’t liable.
“Someone who works in the building broke in using the master key and stole all of my stuff, but I actually don’t know what to do,” a visibly stressed Moon told the camera.

Phillip Upgrades Airbnb, Target Below Price
sum: Phillip Securities has upgraded Airbnb (NASDAQ: ABNB) to Neutral from Reduce and raised its price target to $184 from $158, TheFly reported today. Airbnb runs the online marketplace where hosts rent out homes and guests book stays. The shares will next trade on Monday, so the upgrade has not yet reached the price.

Airbnb closed Friday at $186.78, up 3.12% on the day and 9.79% above its $170.13 close before the results on the 5th of November. The new $184 target sits about 1.5% below that price, and the shares are about 5.6% under their 52-week high of $197.87.

Phillip, a brokerage and research house, now forecasts fiscal 2026 revenue growth of 17% and an adjusted EBITDA margin (operating profit before certain costs, as a share of revenue) of 36%. It points to higher nights and seats booked and lower sales and marketing costs. Airbnb’s own outlook is high-teens growth and a margin of about 36%.

The upgrade follows Airbnb’s third-quarter report, released after the Nasdaq close on the 5th of November. Revenue rose 19% to $4.9bn, against 10% growth a year earlier. Gross booking value, the total value of bookings before Airbnb’s fees, rose 21% to $27.7bn, and earnings per share were $3.16 against a consensus of $2.86. The company also raised its full-year outlook and authorised an extra $12bn buyback. The shares rose 11.67% on the 6th of November to $189.99, though broader market volatility over the period means the results were not the only influence.

Other brokers were already more positive. Oppenheimer raised its target to $230 from $210 and kept Outperform on the 6th of November. Analysts’ mean target is $203.83, with 22 Strong Buy, 4 Buy, 17 Hold and 1 Sell ratings.

Phillip says Airbnb’s newer businesses beyond rentals, which include hotels, services and an AI travel agent planned for the first half of 2027, offer longer-term upside but are unlikely to be material over the next 3-5 years.

Этот значительный рост является результатом расширения внедрения электронной коммерции и увеличения объема цифровых платежей во всем регионе.

Акции Airbnb выросли в ходе торговой сессии, отражая возобновление уверенности инвесторов, подпитываемое устойчивой динамикой спроса на поездки, положительными институциональными потоками и стабилизацией макроэкономических настроений в секторе потребительских товаров. Пока инвесторы переваривают последние квартальные операционные данные, платформа продолжает демонстрировать надежные фундаментальные показатели, особенно в плане трансграничных поездок и ускоренного расширения предложения на международных рынках.

Основным катализатором, поддерживающим акции, является устойчивое состояние бронирования поездок по всему миру и стабилизация средних дневных тарифов. Участники рынка положительно отреагировали на признаки того, что потребительские расходы на активный отдых остаются стабильными, несмотря на более широкую обеспокоенность по поводу дискреционных бюджетов. Airbnb постоянно извлекает выгоду из своего уникального, диверсифицированного предложения с длинным хвостом, которое изолирует его от стандартного циклического давления, с которым сталкиваются традиционные аналоги в сфере жилья. Растущая динамика бронирования и длительного проживания за пределами города еще больше укрепила настроения рынка в отношении многофункционального позиционирования компании.

Что касается операционной деятельности и платформы, стратегические обновления, подчеркивающие качество хоста, прозрачное отображение цен и поисковую оптимизацию на основе искусственного интеллекта, дают ощутимый прирост эффективности. Эти усовершенствования продукта снизили трения со стороны клиентов, повысили коэффициент конверсии и увеличили удержание пользователей. Более того, дисциплинированное управление затратами и непрерывный выкуп акций позволили сохранить генерацию свободного денежного потока, заверив институциональных инвесторов в приверженности руководства возврату капитала при финансировании внедрения продуктов с высокой рентабельностью инвестиций.

items.t: Can Airbnb Stock Compound Your Money?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Airbnb (ABNB) stock returned 50.7% over the past twelve months, against 12.8% for the S&P 500. The company continued to buy back its own shares during that time, and its diluted share count is 9.5% smaller than it was three years ago. This reduction means each share you own holds a larger slice of the business and its profits. So has that bigger slice come with bigger earnings for each share?

Airbnb’s diluted earnings per share fell 13.5% a year between the twelve months ended September 2023 and the twelve months ended September 2026. The company’s net income fell 16.3% a year over the same period. With fewer shares outstanding, each share’s earnings fell more slowly than the profit, but they still fell. The starting point was unusually high, though: the $5.46 billion profit in the twelve months ended September 2023 came on only $2.25 billion of operating income.

The whole fall came in the first of those three years, and per-share earnings have risen in each year since. In the twelve months ended September 2026, Airbnb’s earnings per share rose 27.1%, against 21.9% for its net income. This means each share’s slice grew faster than the profit behind it. The company spent $3.95 billion buying back shares over those twelve months, though the $1.77 billion it paid employees in stock offset part of that total. Net of that stock pay, Airbnb’s buybacks equaled 2.0% of its market value at the November 11, 2026 close.

Airbnb put its free cash flow over the twelve months ended September 2026 at $4.9 billion, more than it spent on buybacks. That cash comes from a booking business that grew faster than a year earlier. Revenue rose 16.7% to $13.9 billion over those same twelve months, and management said hotel bookings accelerated in fiscal Q3 2026.

Airbnb also holds far more cash than debt. The company ended September 2026 with $12.6 billion of cash and short-term investments, against $2.41 billion of debt. On November 5, 2026, management announced that the board had approved a new $12 billion repurchase program, which comes on top of what was left under the existing plan. That new program alone equals about 11% of the company’s $107 billion market value.

sum: - Airbnb held up better than the broader technology market during the Nov. 5 sell-off before jumping following its earnings report.
- Third-quarter revenue rose 19%, bookings accelerated, and management raised its full-year outlook.
- A new $12 billion share repurchase authorization adds to the positive outlook, although valuation and slowing benefits from flexible payments remain considerations.

Thursday, Nov. 5, was one of the market’s roughest sessions in years. The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52%, its worst day since April 2025, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 dropped 6.36%, its steepest decline since March 2020. Selling was driven in part by fears that Democrats’ midterm gains could slow the AI data center buildout, and chip stocks took the brunt, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF NASDAQ: SMH falling by roughly 11%.

Airbnb NASDAQ: ABNB didn’t escape entirely, slipping 3.5% to close at $170.13. But it held up far better than the broader tech market, and it was still up about 3.5% on the week and more than 25% year to date heading into its report. That relative strength made Airbnb's third-quarter earnings release even more interesting. Would the results justify the stock’s outperformance and notable relative strength, or give investors a reason to lock in gains?
At least initially, the answer was clear. Shares jumped about 11% in after-hours trading to trade near $189, within roughly 2% of their 52-week high of $193.45.

Airbnb’s third-quarter revenue rose 19% to $4.87 billion, its fastest growth in more than three years and well ahead of the roughly $4.75 billion analysts expected. Earnings of $3.16 per share also beat the $2.85 consensus by 31 cents, though a lower tax provision flattered the year-over-year comparison.

sum: Airbnb, the popular peer-to-peer home rental platform, has seen its stock surge in after-hours trading, buoyed by a robust performance in the third quarter and optimistic forecasts for the remainder of the year. The company’s CEO, Brian Chesky, celebrated the results, stating, “Airbnb is back in growth mode.” He highlighted the rarity of a marketplace of Airbnb’s magnitude reaccelerating growth, emphasizing the significant momentum the company is experiencing.

In its latest earnings report, Airbnb revealed earnings per share of $3.16, comfortably exceeding Wall Street’s estimated figures of $2.85 per share, as per S&P Global Market Intelligence data. The company’s revenue for the quarter reached $4.87 billion, representing a 19% increase and surpassing analyst expectations of $4.74 billion.

Airbnb reported particularly strong booking figures in North America, noting that nights booked had grown at their fastest pace in four years. The company also acknowledged a notable trend: not only are previous guests returning to the platform, but there is an increase in first-time users discovering the service.

The encouraging results prompted Airbnb to revise its guidance for the fourth quarter, predicting revenue growth of 16% to 19%, which translates to an estimated range of $3.22 billion to $3.28 billion. This forecast also exceeds the midpoint estimate of $3.16 billion projected by analysts. For the full fiscal year, Airbnb anticipates revenue growth in the high teens, alongside an expectation that adjusted EBITDA margins will rise to approximately 36%.

This strong performance underscores the resilience of Airbnb in the face of global travel demand, indicating a positive trajectory as the company continues to capitalize on market trends and consumer preferences.

Airbnb (ABNB) keeps doing the things that move a stock, and the stock keeps not moving. Revenue grew 18% last quarter, management raised guidance, and in May, the company shipped its largest product release ever. Shares still closed at $132.28 on June 12, about 11% lower than five years ago and stuck mid-range between a 52-week low of $110.81 and a high of $147.25.

That is the tension. Airbnb stock 2026 is not a broken-business story. It is a market that has watched the company compound for three years and paid roughly the same price the whole time. Bulls see a platform entering new verticals from a net cash position and call the flat chart a coiled spring. Bears see slowing core growth and call it fair value. The question neither side can answer: what forces the re-rating?
The catalysts are already on the table. They just haven’t shown up in the numbers yet.

On May 7, Airbnb reported Q1 revenue up 18% to $2.7 billion, beating the high end of guidance. Gross booking value, the total dollar value booked on the platform, rose 19% to $29 billion. Free cash flow hit $1.7 billion in the quarter and $4.5 billion over the trailing twelve months, a 36% margin. The next day, the stock rose just 0.73%.

The shrug traces to the guidance. Management raised the full-year outlook but framed growth as accelerating only to “low to mid-teens” and held adjusted EBITDA margin at “at least 35%,” because it plans to keep reinvesting. CFO Ellie Mertz was blunt: “We are actively looking to reinvest to drive growth,” citing marketing, international expansion, and AI. Airbnb is choosing the long game over a clean margin beat, and the market hasn’t decided whether to reward it.

The engine looks healthier than the price suggests. Nights booked on the app grew 22% and now make up 63% of total nights, up from 58% a year ago. First-time bookers grew 10%, the fastest since 2022. Reserve Now, Pay Later, which lets guests book now and pay closer to the stay, drove about 20% of global GBV.

Paris is ground zero for Europe’s backlash against illegal Airbnbs
sum: Early one drizzly morning in Paris, a handful of city officials make their way up a steep, narrow street in the historic neighborhood of Montmartre, with a reporter in tow and the domed Sacré-Coeur basilica looming above. The group stops at an apartment building that looks like any other on the block. It is only when they step inside the entrance hall that anything seems unusual. Signs pasted to the walls declare that loud noise and nighttime gatherings are forbidden. And many of the front doors have metal lockboxes bolted to them, with apartment keys inside. Both are telltale signs that the city workers have found what they’re looking for: illegal Airbnbs.

During the next half-hour, as we climb stairs and knock on doors, a few sleepy residents emerge to complain—not about us, but to us. They describe how their building has begun to feel like a travelers’ crash pad, with rolling suitcases clattering on the pavestones at all hours, and the outdoor courtyard becoming a rowdy tavern on warm evenings. “A living hell,” one calls it.

These modest Montmartre homes are just one flash point in Europe’s growing Airbnb backlash. Even as short-term home rentals have become a global travel norm, more cities worldwide have blamed Airbnb and its competitors for their housing squeeze and affordability crises. In Europe, and in Paris in particular, the growing opposition has gathered real momentum. Paris’s restrictions are among the most rigid, sharply limiting the number of nights that any property can be made available for short-term rentals. The owners of those Montmartre apartments could face fines of well over €100,000 if it’s proved they have violated the law.

“People are buying up properties, becoming a kind of hotelier, developing these businesses that are taking apartments out of the local market,” outgoing Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo fumes over lunch in City Hall’s ornate dining room. Hidalgo, whose term expired in March, describes how she, together with the mayors of Barcelona and Rome, spent years pushing the 27-country European Union to crack down on Airbnb.

items.t: Spanish court orders Airbnb to pay €64 million fine and refuses to suspend sanction
sum: Madrid’s High Court refuses to suspend a €64 million fine on Airbnb by Spain’s Consumer Ministry for illegal holiday rentals and misleading ads; the platform must pay while it appeals.

Airbnb has suffered another setback in the Spanish market. On Monday, the High Court of Justice of Madrid (TSJM) rejected the company’s request for interim measures to suspend payment of the nearly €64 million fine imposed on it by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs in December 2025. As a result of this decision, the platform must pay the penalty while the court case continues.

The ruling does not go into the substance of the case, but simply rejects the company’s request to halt payment until a final judgment is issued. Airbnb, however, still intends to challenge the fine, arguing that it runs counter to the Spanish and European legal framework.

The fine was issued for a number of infringements linked to the publication of tourist accommodation adverts on its platform. Chief among them were the listing of unlicensed properties, the use of false or incorrect registration numbers and the lack of accurate information about hosts, practices that the authorities describe as misleading for consumers.

According to Spain’s Ministry of Consumer Affairs, the amount of the fine is equivalent to six times the illegal profit made through these practices. The irregularities also affected tens of thousands of adverts that breached the regional regulations in force on tourist accommodation.

The government has sought to tighten control over short-term tourist rentals in order to tackle the housing crisis affecting Spain and other major European markets. Other countries, including France, Italy and Portugal, have also toughened their rules in response to the impact on access to housing.

items.t: Airbnb's $2.5 Billion Bond Sale Surprises Market, Sending Shares Lower
sum: Airbnb (ABNB) shares fell sharply on Wednesday after the vacation rental giant announced a surprise $2.5 billion bond offering, a move that caught investors off guard and raised questions about the company's capital strategy. The stock dropped approximately 5% following a Bloomberg report detailing the new debt issuance.

The offering, which marks Airbnb's debut in the investment-grade bond market, consists of 3-, 5-, and 10-year notes. The sale was led by major financial institutions Bank of America (BAC), Goldman Sachs (GS), and Morgan Stanley (MS). The primary impetus for the fundraising is the impending maturity of $2 billion in 0% convertible senior notes on March 15, 2026.

Those zero-interest notes were issued in 2021 with a conversion price of $288.64 per share, a level far above the stock's current trading price. This made the conversion feature effectively worthless, leaving Airbnb with a straightforward $2 billion debt repayment obligation. The new bond sale is widely seen as a refinancing maneuver to address this maturity.

The market's negative reaction stemmed from several key factors. First and foremost, the company is transitioning from a cost-free debt structure to one that carries interest payments. The 2021 convertible notes carried a 0% coupon, providing Airbnb with exceptionally cheap capital during its post-IPO growth phase. The new bonds, while investment-grade, will introduce a recurring interest expense, signaling a rise in the company's overall cost of capital.

Secondly, Airbnb's strong liquidity position gave investors pause. The company holds over $11 billion in liquid assets, a substantial financial cushion. This led analysts and shareholders to question the immediate necessity of raising an additional $2.5 billion through debt, especially given the company's recent focus on reducing leverage and returning capital to shareholders via stock buybacks.

Finally, the unexpected nature of the sale sparked concerns about a potential shift in financial strategy. The move would nearly double Airbnb's current debt load, moving away from what many perceived as a capital-light, balance sheet-conservative approach that had been in place for the past few years.

sum: Vacation rentals offer many potential benefits compared with hotel rooms, including lower prices, more amenities and a more personal touch. Yet knowing which vacation rental platform provides the best overall experience for travelers is another question.

There is a clear winner between Airbnb versus Vrbo: Airbnb. Our analysis found that Airbnb offers a better overall experience for most travelers. That said, the right booking platform for you will depend on your travel preferences.
The biggest difference between these two platforms is the type of accommodation they offer:
- Vrbo offers stand-alone vacation homes only. It doesn't generally offer “shared” spaces like private rooms or more unusual options like campsites.
- Airbnb offers stand-alone vacation homes as well as shared spaces and even hotel rooms. Although it started as a home-sharing concept, it now hosts many types of accommodations.

In other words, if you’re looking for a home to rent for a family get-together, both Airbnb and Vrbo are good choices. But if you’re looking for a cheaper shared space or something less typical, stick with Airbnb.

If you’ve had bad luck with vacation rentals in the past, which were dumpier or dirtier than the pictures suggested, you might consider searching for Airbnb “Plus” properties, which have been vetted in person for quality.
